questions.title: How exactly is the entropy patching threshold selected to achieve a target average patch size?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.3 the paper describes using a global entropy threshold \(\theta_g\) or a relative entropy change threshold \(\theta_r\) to decide patch boundaries. It also mentions estimating a threshold that yields a desired average patch size on the pre‑training data, but it is unclear how this estimation is performed. Do the authors compute the empirical distribution of next‑byte entropies on a validation split and then perform a binary search for \(\theta_g\) (or \(\theta_r\)) that gives the target mean patch length? How is the “average patch size” defined when patches have variable lengths, and is any smoothing applied to avoid highly volatile boundaries?

questions.title: Why does the cross‑attention module in the encoder pool only over bytes belonging to a single patch?
questions.question_body: The encoder cross‑attention (Section 4.1) uses queries for each patch that attend only to keys/values from bytes inside that patch. Intuitively, one might think allowing a query to attend to a larger window of surrounding bytes could give richer context before forming the latent representation. What is the justification for this strict per‑patch attention mask? Does it limit the ability of the latent transformer to capture dependencies that span across patch boundaries, or are those handled solely by the global transformer’s block‑causal attention?

questions.title: What is the role of the n‑gram hash embeddings and how are they combined with byte embeddings?
questions.question_body: Section 4.1.1 introduces hash‑based embeddings for byte n‑grams (n=3…8) which are added to the byte embedding and then normalized. I am confused about several points: (1) why use a hash function rather than a learned lookup table for each n‑gram? (2) How is the normalization performed – is it simply dividing by the number of n‑gram contributions plus one? (3) Do these hash embeddings get updated during training like regular parameters, and how large are the hash tables in practice?

questions.title: How does incremental patching differ from BPE tokenization in terms of determinism during generation?
questions.question_body: The paper defines incremental patching as satisfying \(f_p(\mathbf{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\mathbf{x})_{<i}\). It then claims BPE does not satisfy this property because tokenization can depend on future bytes. Could someone provide a concrete example where a prefix yields different BPE tokenizations depending on its continuation, and contrast that with how BLT decides patch boundaries at generation time without seeing future bytes?

questions.title: Why does the FLOPs per byte equation include a term \(V=256\) only for the decoder?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.5, FLOPs per byte are summed over encoder, global transformer, decoder, and cross‑attention components. The decoder term multiplies \(\text{Transf.FL}(h_{\mathcal{D}}, l_{\mathcal{D}}, m_{\mathcal{D}}, V=256)\). I assume \(V\) stands for vocabulary size for the output projection, but why is this term omitted for the encoder and global transformer? Are those modules truly vocabulary‑free, or is there an implicit assumption that their output dimension does not depend on \(V\)?

questions.title: Can you clarify how ‘patch size’ interacts with context length during training and inference?
questions.question_body: The authors state that larger average patch sizes reduce inference FLOPs because fewer latent transformer steps are needed, yet they also keep “the number of bytes in each batch constant in expectation”. How is the context window (in bytes) adjusted when changing average patch size? For example, if we move from an average patch size of 4 bytes to 8 bytes, does the model see half as many patches per batch, and are other hyperparameters (e.g., attention window width in local models) scaled accordingly?

questions.title: What is meant by ‘entropy drift’ and how does resetting the entropy model context mitigate it?
questions.question_body: Section 4.2 mentions that entropy drift occurs when using a large context for entropy estimation, especially on repetitive data like multiple‑choice tasks. How does extending the context cause drift in next‑byte entropy estimates, and why does resetting the entropy model’s context with newlines help? Is this related to distribution shift between training and inference contexts?

questions.title: How does BLT’s global latent transformer handle long‑range dependencies across patches?
questions.question_body: Since most computation on raw bytes happens in lightweight local encoders/decoders, I am worried that information spanning many patches might be lost before reaching the global transformer. The global model uses block‑causal attention over patches – does this provide enough capacity to model dependencies across distant patches (e.g., coreference across paragraphs), or would increasing its depth be necessary as patch size grows?

questions.title: Why do larger patch sizes (e.g., 8 bytes) initially underperform but eventually overtake token‑based models at higher scales?
questions.question_body: Figure 5 shows that BLT with average patch size 8 starts worse than BPE at 1 B parameters but catches up and surpasses it by ~7 B. Is this because larger patches reduce the relative cost of the local encoder/decoder, allowing more FLOPs to be allocated to the global transformer as we scale parameters? Or does it reflect better utilization of compute due to fewer latent steps despite decreased granularity?

questions.title: What are the practical implications of using FlexAttention for dynamic cross‑attention masks?
questions.question_body: "Flex Attention" is mentioned as required for cross‑attention where masks depend on dynamic patch boundaries. How does FlexAttention differ from standard fused kernels like FlashAttention in terms of performance and memory usage? Are there any limitations (e.g., maximum sequence length or number of heads) that could affect scalability of BLT on large GPUs?
